title: Already or not yet — the করেছি form
goal: Say that something has already happened, and learn a negative that looks nothing like the one you know: -নি, which means both “not yet” and “didn't”.
bekal: form the perfect: করেছি, গেছি, খেয়েছি
negate it with the tail -নি, not with না
tell খেলাম (ate yesterday) from খেয়েছি (have eaten)
answer the greeting ভাত খেয়েছেন? naturally

dialogs.title: কথোপকথন — Home late
dialogs.intro: Ani gets home at nine at night and finds Mitali still waiting in the dining room. Notice Mitali's first question — in Bengal, that's the real greeting.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: No, I haven't eaten yet. It got too late.
lines.literal: no, still — not-eaten. late — become — has-gone.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: I knew it! That's why I haven't eaten either. Come on.
lines.literal: I — knew! that's-why — I-too — not-eaten. come-on.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: Of course. Eating alone is no fun.
lines.literal: of-course. alone — to-eat — good — feel — not.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.literal: yes. mother — today — hilsa — cooking — has-done.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: Then today your life will change!
lines.literal: then — today — your — life — change — will-go!

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: I've heard it has lots of bones. Will I manage?
lines.literal: bone — many — have-heard. I — will-manage — right?

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: Eat slowly. I'll show you how.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: You've done so much for me, sister.
lines.literal: you(polite) — my — for — much — have-done, sister.

notes: ⚠️ **ভাত খেয়েছেন? isn't just a question — it's a greeting.** Literally “have you eaten rice?”, but it means something closer to “how are you?” and “I care about you”. Many Asian languages share this habit, so think of it as a warm “how are you doing?”. A natural answer: **হ্যাঁ, খেয়েছি** or **না, এখনো খাইনি**, and the question is often followed by a sincere offer of food.

**The perfect is made by inserting -েছ- before the usual ending:** করি → কর**েছি**, করেন → কর**েছেন**, করে → কর**েছে**. Exactly the pattern of Unit 8, just with a different infix. ⚠️ Verbs ending in a vowel insert -য়ে-: খাওয়া → **খেয়েছি**, দেওয়া → **দিয়েছি**, পাওয়া → **পেয়েছি**, হওয়া → **হয়েছে**. And যাওয়া shortens to **গেছি**.

⚠️ **The negative doesn't use না at all.** The right form is the tail **-নি** attached to the present-tense stem: খেয়েছি → **খাইনি** (haven't eaten), গেছি → **যাইনি**, দেখেছি → **দেখিনি**, শুনেছি → **শুনিনি**. Note that the stem goes back to the present form — খাই + নি, যাই + নি. This is one of the most frequently botched forms, so learn it as a pair: **খেয়েছি ↔ খাইনি**.

⚠️ **And -নি means both “not yet” and “didn't” in the past.** আমি যাইনি can mean “I haven't gone yet” or “I didn't go”. To stress “not yet”, add **এখনো** *èkhôno*: আমি এখনো যাইনি. To stress “never”, add **কখনো** *kôkhôno*: আমি কখনো খাইনি (I've never eaten it).

**When to use খেলাম and when খেয়েছি?** **খেলাম** is for an event finished at a specific time in the past — কাল দুপুরে ভাত খেলাম. **খেয়েছি** is for something that has happened and **still matters now** — আমি খেয়েছি (I've eaten, so I'm not hungry). The difference matches English “I ate” versus “I've eaten”.

**হয়ে গেছে — “it's gone and happened”.** Bengali often attaches **যাওয়া** after another verb to show that a change is complete and can't be undone: দেরি হয়ে গেছে (it's already too late), ভুলে গেছি (I've gone and forgotten), ঘুমিয়ে গেছে (he/she has fallen asleep). ⚠️ This pattern is very common, and it has nothing to do with “going”.

⚠️ **ইলিশ — hilsa fish — deserves respect.** It is the national fish of Bangladesh, very bony, very rich, and considered the peak of Bengali cooking. Eating it is a skill of its own: the bones are separated with the tongue, not the hands. If you choke once, no one will tease you; but praise it sincerely and you'll be remembered for years.

grammars.title: The perfect and its negative
after: **For the more distant past — “had already …” — add ছিল:** করেছিলাম, গিয়েছিলাম, খেয়েছিলাম. ⚠️ This form is used for events finished **before** another past event, and for the distant past: ছোটবেলায় আমি ঢাকায় গিয়েছিলাম (as a child I once went to Dhaka).

grammars.title: Already, not yet, and ever
after: ⚠️ **কী হয়েছে? is a sentence you'll hear often and need often** — “what's up?”, “what happened?” or “what's wrong?”. Said gently, it shows concern; said quickly, it's an urgent question.

head: Sentence
Say it
When to use it
rows: Everyday greeting — not really about food.
Keeping well? — a greeting to elders.

blocks.title: ⚠️ On answering small talk
items: **চলছে** *chôlchhé* — “it's moving” — is the most typically Bengali answer to “how are you?”. It means “so-so, life goes on”, and is used far more than “very well”. Answering দারুণ! (great!) every time actually sounds overdone.
**Questions about family aren't nosy.** বাড়ির সবাই ভালো? is a required part of greeting someone you know, and not asking can feel cold. Just answer **সবাই ভালো, আপনার?**
**অনেক দিন পর!** is used even if you met just a week ago. It's not a statement about time but an expression of delight — like “where have you been?!”.

blocks.text: One thing worth keeping from this unit. The **-েছি** form is the past form you'll hear most in real conversation, far more often than the -লাম form. The reason is simple: everyday talk is more about what **has** happened and still matters than about logging events at a point in time. If you can master only one past form first, choose this one.

exercises.prompt: Change into the perfect for আমি.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: আমি খাইনি। — সে আসেনি। — আমি দেখিনি। — আমরা যাইনি।
আপনি কি ভাত খেয়েছেন? — আমি এখনো খাইনি। — দেরি হয়ে গেছে। — আমি কখনো ইলিশ খাইনি। — আপনি আমার জন্য অপেক্ষা করেছেন।
ভাত খেয়েছেন? — না, এখনো খাইনি। — আমি কখনো ঢাকায় যাইনি। — সে এখনো আসেনি। — কী হয়েছে? — আমি ভুলে গেছি।
